identical work. Guarded in the BACKEND rather than by disabling the button:
that is the one place every trigger has to pass through, and a UI-only guard
narrows the race instead of closing it. A second trigger now returns the running
job id, so the caller watches that run instead of starting a duplicate. No new
state — JobTracker already records kind and status.

The strip inferred "indexing them now" from the auto-index PREFERENCE alone,
so it claimed work was happening even when the run had already failed, or was
never started because nothing had changed. `ai_embedding_status` now reports
whether an embedding job is actually running and the strip reads that.

And the step's top doc comment still said the switch "defaults ON" while the
code — and a comment twelve lines below it — did the opposite. Left over from
the first draft; the opt-in behaviour is the correct one, so the comment was
what needed fixing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: make the embed-job claim atomic and the completion listener race-proof

Two review findings, and closing the second surfaced a harder race than the one
reported.

The guard was check-then-act: `running_embed_job` then `job_start` are two
separate lock acquisitions, so two commands can both observe "nothing running"
before either registers. Scan and insert now share one lock via
`JobTracker::start_exclusive`.

That returns `Option`, not `Result`. R6 caught the first attempt for banning
`Result<_, String>`, and the rule was pointing at a real modelling error: "a job
is already running" is not a failure, it is the job the caller should watch. The
type says that now.

The completion listener compared against the `inFlightJob` STATE.
`setInFlightJob` only schedules a render, so a job finishing before that render
commits hits a closure still holding `null`, drops its own completion, and
latches the guard forever — auto-indexing dead until restart. Now compared
against a ref written synchronously alongside the state, the same fix
`EmbeddingsSettings` already documents for `reindexJobIdRef`.

Writing the regression test for that exposed a second ordering: a job can finish
before the invoke that created it even RESOLVES (an index where every document
fails returns almost immediately), so the completion arrives before there is any
claim to match. The ref alone does not help there. Terminal ids seen without a
claim are now remembered briefly, and a claim for one of them releases
immediately instead of waiting for an event that already passed.

Both races are pinned, and both tests were verified to fail against the previous
code rather than assumed to.

fix: make clicking an OS notification open the app, on the right screen (#949)

* fix: make clicking an os notification open the app, on the right screen

Reported twice: clicking a Windows notification does nothing, and there was no
way to jump from a notification to the thing it was about.

Both had one cause. `tauri-plugin-notification`'s desktop `show()` is
notify-rust fire-and-forget, and the `onAction` JS helper its docs point at for
clicks resolves to `plugin:notification|register_listener` — a command the
plugin registers ONLY on mobile (its desktop invoke_handler is exactly notify,
request_permission, is_permission_granted). So the renderer's subscription
failed with "Command not found" on every desktop startup and no banner click
ever reached the app. `notifications_clicked` — which already does the right
thing — had no caller other than the tray.

Show the banner natively instead, per platform, since only Windows is
callback-based:

- Windows: tauri-winrt-notification's on_activated, non-blocking.
- macOS/Linux: notify-rust's wait_for_action BLOCKS, so it runs on
  spawn_blocking. Linux additionally needs a declared `default` action for a
  body click to be delivered at all.

Both crates were already in the tree transitively; they are pinned to the
locked versions so there is no duplicate copy.

Routing: the click now carries the clicked notification's OWN route, so
"Autopilot X found 3 jobs" opens THAT autopilot rather than a list to search.
Every notification source already attached a route (autopilot -> /autopilot with
its id) and the bell already followed it — only the OS banner didn't. Validated
through the same resolveNotificationRoute the bell uses, so an unknown backend
route falls back instead of breaking navigation. A tray click sends no route and
still just opens the inbox.

The dead renderer seam (onOsBannerClick) is removed, which also silences the
startup console error it produced.

Known limit, all platforms: the callback lives in this process, so it fires only
while the app runs. A click after the app exits needs a COM activator on Windows
and is out of scope.

* fix: close two holes that made architecture rule r15 miss real leaks

R15 shipped in this PR with an empty allowlist, which read as "the codebase is
clean". It was partly "the scanner cannot see it":

1. The marker list held only fully-qualified calls (`log::warn!(`), so the three
   modules that do `use tracing::warn;` and call `warn!(…)` — extraction/mod,
   extraction/pdf, extraction/registry — were silently exempt. Match the bare
   forms too.
2. The span heuristic ended at the first line ending in `);`, documented as
   "the outer call's own close". Not always: a macro argument holding a block or
   closure can contain a statement ending in `);` at a deeper indent, which
   truncated the span before the real `.display()` one line further down.
   Require the close to be at an indent no deeper than the macro's own line.

passes over the whole crate with an empty allowlist — now meaning it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

* fix: cap generation error messages in the log instead of dropping them

The AI review flagged the two generation-failure log lines as the same
CWE-532 shape as the export ones and asked for errorClass. That fix is wrong
here, and the asymmetry is the point.

An export failure can lose its message safely because the Rust side already
logs the critical issue CODES — the reason survives elsewhere. A generation
failure has no second record: "Ollama 500: the input length exceeds the context
length" is the ONLY trace of why a run died, and it is precisely the line that
would have resolved the macOS report this PR exists for in one look. Reducing it
to "Error" would delete the reason this logging was added.

So keep the message, bounded to 300 chars — the same cap friendly_cli_error
already applies to captured CLI stderr. A provider or transport error is short;
a response that has somehow captured document text is not, and the cap stops
that spilling wholesale. redact_lines strips URLs, paths and credential
assignments as the bundle is written, but does NOT redact prose, which is
exactly the gap this cap covers.

Truncation is marked, not silent — an unmarked cut reads as a complete provider
error that merely ends oddly.

* fix: persist the embedding format version on cached posting vectors

`get_posting_vector` synthesised `version: EMBEDDING_VECTOR_VERSION` when

incapable of ever rejecting a row from this table. Freshness rested
entirely on a hand-maintained invariant: every future format bump had to

* fix: bound what happens after the cap, not just the read

Security review of this branch found the sweep's own claim was false in one
place. The LinkedIn client deliberately disables reqwest decompression and
gunzips by hand, so capping the read bounded only the compressed bytes —
8 MB in, up to ~8 GB resident. Both decode sites now bound the decompressed
side too and reject a payload that lands exactly on the cap.

Also: a discarded `.text()` read in the same file the sweep converted;
`read_json_capped` rebuilt on `from_slice` so it stops charset-sniffing
(JSON is UTF-8 by RFC 8259, and a gateway mislabelling it as iso-8859-1 was
turning valid bodies into schema errors); its parse-failure log now emits
position rather than serde's message, which would embed the offending body
value once a call site deserializes into anything but `Value`.

Two test fixes: the cap test used one oversized chunk, so it passed
identically against a per-chunk guard — it now drives three small chunks
through the shared accumulator, verified by temporarily breaking the guard.
And the migration idempotency test now rolls `user_version` back, because
`run_migrations` skips on `current >= version`, so the guard it claimed to
re-exercise never ran twice.

The new column defaults to 2, not 0. Every surviving row post-dates the
v1 to v2 eviction wipe, so it is provably current — defaulting to 0 would
have re-embedded the whole posting cache for no correctness gain. The
literal must not track future bumps; it records what rows were at migration
time.
